collection: Primary4 English reading evidence, letters and conditional vowel contrast
note: Twenty-two original structured drafts:17 written interpretation tasks, four observed read-aloud tasks and one conditional listening task. Four original reading passages and one original fictional letter. Six new author-proposed mappings; all academic review pending. No actual audio or learner performance claimed.

questions.subject: English Studies
questions.learningObjective: Read class-appropriate passages on topical issues.
questions.prompt: Read Learning the Fold aloud to a teacher. Use pauses to make the sequence clear. Afterwards, explain in your own words what Hauwa checked before her container could stand.
questions.answer: A successful reading keeps the words and event order clear, with useful pauses. Hauwa compared the last fold/corner with the example and corrected the corner tucked on the wrong side.
questions.explanation: Read-aloud performance is an original assessment route for the reading objective, not a prescribed national fluency rate.

markingGuide.description: Reads accurately enough to preserve the passage’s meaning, allowing self-correction.
Uses intelligible phrasing and pauses.
Explains the checked/corrected corner in her own words.

questions.passage:
Learning the Fold
At the class craft table, Hauwa tried to fold a paper container. She watched the demonstration and quickly copied the first two folds. Her container looked neat, but it would not stand upright. Instead of starting with another sheet, she opened the last fold and compared it with the teacher’s example. One corner was tucked on the wrong side. Hauwa corrected it and marked that step on a small practice card. When her friend asked for help, she showed the tricky corner slowly. By the end of the lesson, Hauwa could explain the step without looking at the card. She had learnt more from checking one mistake than from hiding it.

questions.passage:
The Practice Question
Tomi’s study group usually read their notes silently and then put the books away. Before a class quiz, Zainab suggested a different plan. Each pupil wrote one question about the lesson. They exchanged the questions, answered them without looking at the notes, and then checked the explanations together. When two answers disagreed, the group returned to the relevant paragraph instead of choosing the loudest speaker. Tomi discovered that he could remember a definition but could not explain its example. He marked that part for more practice. The group did not promise that everyone would get full marks. They wanted to find out what each person still needed to understand.

questions.prompt: Read A Sign for the Paper Bin aloud as an informational report. Afterwards, explain what the new sign was meant to improve.
questions.answer: The learner reads clearly, preserving the distinction between the initial problem and the reported change. The sign was meant to help users put only the accepted clean scrap paper into that collection.
questions.explanation: This is a fictional school-specific collection rule, not a universal recycling policy or an instruction to pupils to handle waste.

markingGuide.description: Reads the report accurately enough for meaning.
Uses suitable phrasing for the informational sequence.
Explains the purpose of the clearer sign.

questions.passage:
A Sign for the Paper Bin
At a fictional school, a labelled bin was provided for clean scrap paper from classroom activities. At first, some pupils put empty drink cartons and wet food wrappers into it as well. The caretaker explained that these items did not belong in that particular paper collection. The environment club made a clearer sign, using examples of the paper the school accepted. A pupil checked the bin at the end of each club session and asked an adult for help if unsuitable items were found. The club’s report said that the clearer sign reduced mistakes. It did not claim that one bin had solved every litter problem in the school.

questions.answer: The learner reads clearly and explains that the arrangement aims to let energetic and quiet activities share school space without one unnecessarily disturbing the other.

markingGuide.description: Reads with sufficient accuracy and intelligibility.

questions.passage:
Quiet Areas, Different Needs
A school’s environment club observed that pupils used the courtyard in different ways. Some played energetic games during break. Others wanted a place to read or talk quietly. The club did not ask everyone to remain silent throughout break. Instead, it proposed keeping noisy games near the playing field and reserving a small shaded corner for quieter activities. Teachers helped the pupils choose clear signs for both areas. After a trial week, the club invited comments about whether the arrangement worked. The report described this as a plan to share space more thoughtfully, not a rule that one kind of activity was always better than another.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the meaning of an informal letter.
questions.prompt: A fictional pupil writes to a cousin to describe a family celebration and ask about the cousin’s holiday. Explain why this is an informal letter.
questions.answer: It is a personal letter to a relative about shared or everyday experiences, written in a friendly rather than an official style.
questions.explanation: An informal letter is defined by personal purpose, relationship and style; it still needs clear organisation.

markingGuide.description: Identifies the personal relationship/purpose.
Explains a friendly personal style rather than official business.

questions.deliveryNote: Written interpretation of supplied original material; not evidence of observed oral, dictionary or digital performance.

questions.subject: English Studies
questions.learningObjective: Explain the meaning of an informal letter.
questions.prompt: A classmate says an informal letter is simply a letter with no rules and no clear order. Correct that explanation.
questions.answer: An informal letter is a personal, friendly letter, often to a friend or relative. It can still have an address, date, greeting, organised body, closing and sender’s name.
questions.explanation: Informal does not mean careless, unreadable or structure-free.

markingGuide.description: Gives a suitable personal/friendly meaning.
Explains that clear structure and features still matter.

questions.subject: English Studies
questions.topic: Aural Discrimination in Vowels and Consonants
questions.subtopic: Vowel contrast in a stated model
questions.learningObjective: Discriminate vowel sounds in heard words using an explicit prechecked reference model.
questions.prompt: Listen to the teacher’s reference words A and B, then to four test words. After each test word, say A or B to show which reference vowel it matches. Do not read the teacher’s word list.
questions.answer: B, A, A, B.
questions.explanation: This is listening discrimination in a stated non-rhotic British reference model: A has /ʌ/ as in bud; B has /ɜː/ as in bird. It does not assess whether the learner’s own accent must use those realisations. The source typography /˄/ and /3:/ is reconciled explicitly rather than treated as a universal accent rule.

markingGuide.description: Matches the first two test vowels to B then A.
Matches the last two test vowels to A then B.

questions.deliveryNote: Require live or recorded individual evidence. A teacher prepares and checks the task, allows appropriate practice and scores intelligibility and the specified reading/listening features. A written script alone is insufficient. Actual classroom delivery, pronunciation model, recording arrangements and examiner calibration remain unverified. Do not penalise unrelated accent features or impose an invented reading-speed threshold.
questions.examinerScript: Precondition: a qualified teacher must establish an audible, consistent non-rhotic British reference contrast /ʌ/ versus /ɜː/, using an appropriate verified model before scoring. Cambridge indexed pronunciation entries support bud /bʌd/ and bird /bɜːd/; their full pages/audio were not retrieved in this run. If the model, hearing conditions or learner access needs prevent a fair contrast task, postpone rather than infer ability from spelling. During practice, say A: bud and B: bird; explain that the pupil matches vowel sounds, not meanings. Keep spellings, IPA and the key hidden during the test. Read the four test words naturally twice in this order: bird, bud, bud, bird. Permit spoken A/B labels. Do not judge the learner’s natural pronunciation or substitute r-colouring as the cue.
